news.title: National flu and COVID-19 surveillance report: 29 October 2026 (week 44) - GOV.UK
news.rss_summary_html: National flu and COVID-19 surveillance report: 29 October 2026 (week 44)  GOV.UK
news.excerpt_original: National flu and COVID-19 surveillance report: 29 October 2026 (week 44) GOV.UK
news.priority_tier_reason: 政府、WHO/CDC/ECDC或其他官方公共卫生来源
news.content_title: National flu and COVID-19 surveillance report: 29 October 2026 (week 44)
news.content: This publication is licensed under the terms of the Open Government Licence v3.0 except where otherwise stated. To view this licence, visit nationalarchives.gov.uk/doc/open-government-licence/version/3 or write to the Information Policy Team, The National Archives, Kew, London TW9 4DU, or email: psi@nationalarchives.gov.uk . Where we have identified any third party copyright information you will need to obtain permission from the copyright holders concerned. This publication is available at https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/national-flu-and-covid-19-surveillance-reports-2026-to-2027-season/national-flu-and-covid-19-surveillance-report-29-october-2026-week-44 This report summarises the information from the surveillance systems which are used to monitor COVID-19 (caused by severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2)), influenza, respiratory syncytial virus ( RSV ) and diseases caused by other seasonal respiratory viruses in England. This report is based on data up to and including week 43 of 2026 (19 October and 25 October 2026). The main messages of this report are: Annual reports for the 2025 to 2026 season: Influenza in the UK, annual epidemiological report: winter 2025 to 2026 (published 28 May 2026) Epidemiology of COVID-19 in England (published 25 June 2026) Seasonal influenza vaccine uptake in all GP patients: annual report 2025 to 2026 (published 28 May 2026) Seasonal influenza vaccine uptake in school-aged children: annual report 2025 to 2026 (published 28 May 2026) Seasonal influenza vaccine uptake in frontline healthcare workers: annual report 2025 to 2026 (published 28 May 2026) Influenza activity was stable across most indicators and is circulating at low levels. Emergency department ( ED ) attendances for influenza-like-illness ( ILI ) increased and were above seasonally expected levels. The number of influenza-confirmed acute respiratory infection ( ARI ) incidents increased compared with the previous week. Weekly influenza vaccine uptake for the 2026 to 2027 season is reported for the fourth time this season. Data is for week 43 (up to 25 October 2026). Influenza vaccination data was unavailable or incomplete at the time of analysis in weeks 41 and 42, and led to several cohorts not being published in week 42. This has been corrected for this week’s report (week 43), and all cohorts are included. This will be corrected retrospectively in the report for week 42. There remains an issue that affects the attribution of vaccinations by provider setting. This is not expected to affect overall vaccination uptake estimates, which are considered to remain an accurate reflection of the influenza vaccination programme. Compared with the equivalent week last season (week 43 data, 2025 to 2026), vaccine uptake is lower among patients aged 65 years and over (53.6% vs 56.9%), patients aged 6 months to under 65 years in clinical risk groups (24.8% vs 26.2%), those aged 2 years (29.7% vs 30.8%), and those aged 3 years (29.5% vs 30.7%). Vaccine uptake is higher among pregnant women (29.1% vs 27.8%). COVID-19 activity decreased and is circulating at low levels. ED attendances for COVID-19-like illness decreased. The number of COVID-19 confirmed acute respiratory infections ( ARI ) incidents decreased compared with the previous week. By the end of week 43 2026, 42.5% of all people aged 75 years and over in England had been vaccinated with an autumn 2026 dose. Similarly, 18.2% of all people aged under 75 years with a weakened immune system in England had been vaccinated with an autumn 2026 dose since 1 October 2026. RSV activity increased and is circulating at baseline levels. ED attendances for acute bronchiolitis were stable and below seasonally expected levels. Note 1: these indicators use the moving epidemic method ( MEM ) and the mean standard deviation method ( MSD ) to define thresholds to determine their respective levels of activity. Further information on these methods can be found in Influenza surveillance in Europe: establishing epidemic thresholds by the Moving Epidemic Method and Setting thresholds to determine COVID-19 activity levels using the mean standard deviation ( MSD ) method, England, 2022 to 2024 . The MEM approach is well-established for some influenza surveillance indicators, however, for other indicators both the MEM and MSD are experimental and may be subject to future revision. Influenza laboratory surveillance and GP swabbing positivity have transitioned from using MEM to using MSD . These approaches will be considered alongside expert opinion and triangulation of other data sources. The Second Generation Surveillance System ( SGSS ) captures test result information for notifiable infectious diseases, including COVID-19 and influenza, from laboratories in England. The unified sample dataset ( USD ) stores all SARS-CoV-2 test results reported to SGSS , Respiratory DataMart and UKHSA laboratories, and is used to calculate the percentage of tests positive for SARS-CoV-2 among all SARS-CoV-2 tests conducted. As of 27 October 2026, there were a total of 1,847 COVID-19 cases identified in hospital settings in week 43, decreasing from 2,151 cases in the previous week. SARS-CoV-2 (COVID-19) PCR positivity in hospital settings decreased slightly in week 43, with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 8.3% up to Sunday 25 October 2026 compared with 8.8% for the same period on the previous Sunday. Positivity rates were highest among those aged 85 years and over with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 11.1% up to Sunday 25 October 2026. This has decreased compared to 13.0% in the same age group on the previous Sunday. Note 2: data from previous seasons is aligned by day. Note 3: testing policy and practice may change over time which can impact positivity rates, therefore comparisons over time should be interpreted with caution. Notable changes in testing policy occurred during 2022 to 2023, which are outlined in the data quality report . Note 4: the highlighted line corresponds to the age group in the subplot title, grey lines correspond to all other age groups. Influenza positivity remained stable in week 43, with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 6.6% up to Sunday 25 October 2026. This is compared with 6.4% on the previous Sunday. By type, influenza A positivity increased slightly in week 43, with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 5.8% up to Sunday 25 October 2026. Influenza B positivity increased in the same week, with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 0.3% up to Sunday 25 October 2026. Influenza A positivity rates were highest among those aged between 5 and 11 years, with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 16.6% up to Sunday 25 October 2026. This has increased from 11.3% in the same age group on the previous Sunday. Influenza B positivity rates for the same period were highest among those aged between 5 and 11 years, with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 1.8%. This has decreased from 2.3% in the same age group on the previous Sunday. RSV swab-positivity based PCR test results reported through SGSS have been included as a pilot indicator from week 49 2025 onwards. RSV positivity increased in week 43, with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 1.6% up to Sunday 25 October 2026, compared with 1.1% up to the previous Sunday. RSV positivity rates were highest in those aged between 0 and 4 years with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 10.1% up to Sunday 25 October 2026 in week 43. This has increased from 7.8% in the same age group on the previous Sunday. Respiratory DataMart is a sentinel laboratory-based surveillance system where participating laboratories report positive and negative test results for a number of respiratory viruses from samples primarily taken in hospital. A small proportion of primary care samples are also included in this reporting. In week 43, data is based on reporting from 9 out of the 14 sentinel laboratories. In week 43, 4,070 respiratory specimens reported through the Respiratory DataMart System were tested for influenza. There were 258 positive samples for influenza: 179 influenza A (not subtyped), 11 influenza A (H3N2), 51 influenza A (H1N1)pdm09, and 19 influenza B. Overall, influenza positivity increased slightly to 6.3% in week 43 compared with 5.9% in the previous week. In week 43, 4,952 respiratory specimens reported through the Respiratory DataMart System were tested for SARS-CoV-2. There were 376 positive samples for SARS-CoV-2. SARS-CoV-2 positivity remained stable at 7.6% compared with 7.3% in the previous week, with the highest positivity in those aged between 65 and 79 years at 10.0%. RSV positivity increased to 1.5%, with the highest positivity in those aged under 5 years at 8.3%. Adenovirus positivity increased to 1.5%, with the highest positivity in those aged under 5 years at 5.1%. Human metapneumovirus ( hMPV ) positivity decreased to 0.1%, with the highest positivity in those aged between 15 and 44 years at 0.4%. Parainfluenza positivity decreased slightly to 2.9%, with the highest positivity in those aged between 5 and 14 years at 11.3%. Rhinovirus positivity decreased slightly to 16.5%, with the highest positivity in those aged under 5 years at 29.1%. DataMart data is provisional and subject to retrospective updates. Note 5: shading represents 95% confidence intervals. This section is updated fortnightly. Data below was last updated in the week 43 report. UKHSA conducts genomic surveillance of SARS-CoV-2 lineages. This section provides an overview of circulating lineages in England, derived from data on sequenced PCR -positive SARS-CoV-2 samples in SGSS . The prevalence of UKHSA -designated lineages among sequenced cases is presented in Figure 13. To account for reporting delays, we report the proportion of lineages within COVID-19 cases that have had a sequenced positive sample between 14 September 2026 and 27 September 2026. Note that low sequencing numbers, especially within the latest reporting period, will impact the accuracy of the prevalence estimates. These most recent figures should therefore be interpreted with caution. Note that lineages will be grouped independently from their parent lineage once they reach sufficient prevalence, and may be re-grouped into their parent lineage if their prevalence subsequently falls. The data quality report contains more information on lineage groupings. Analysis of viruses from primary and secondary care shows that circulating A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses show low genetic diversity and all belong to clade D.3.1.1. Observations published from the WHO influenza vaccine composition meeting (VCM) in September 2026 suggest low reactivity of some viruses within the D.3.1.1 subclade with post-infection ferret antisera raised against A/Missouri/11/2025 (H1N1)pdm09-like virus – the A(H1N1)pdm09 component in 2026 Southern and 2026/2027 Northern Hemisphere cell- and egg-based influenza vaccines - and human sera post-vaccination with the Southern Hemisphere vaccine 2026. It is not yet clear how vaccine effectiveness against clinical disease may be affected by these observations. Vaccines typically still provide protection against severe clinical disease when drifted strains are seen with only a modest reduction in effectiveness. The characterisation of circulating A(H3N2) viruses shows that A(H3N2) viruses are currently showing low genetic diversity. All sequenced viruses to date belong to genetic subclade K. To date, only a small number of influenza B viruses have been detected, which show some genetic diversity. Between week 35 2026 (week ending 30 August 2026) and week 43 2026 (week ending 25 October 2026), the UKHSA respiratory virus unit ( RVU ) has genetically characterised 297 seasonal influenza viruses, and identified 184 influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses, 86 influenza A(H3N2) viruses, and 27 influenza B viruses. Details of the characterised viruses by subtype are shown in Tables 1, 2 and 3. The RVU has confirmed by genome sequencing the detection of live attenuated influenza vaccine ( LAIV ) viruses in 11 influenza A/B positive samples, collected from children aged between 2 and 16 years. UKHSA RVU performs antigenic characterisation of influenza A(H1N1)pdm09, influenza A(H3N2) and influenza B viruses using haemagglutination inhibition ( HI ) assays. Data from these assays are used to compare how similar the currently circulating influenza viruses are to the strains included in seasonal influenza vaccines, and to monitor for changes in circulating influenza viruses. Similarity of currently circulating influenza strains to vaccine strains is defined as having an antibody titre within 4-fold when compared with reference viruses representative of the vaccine strain. Antigenic characterisation of viruses in the current reporting period is underway. A(H1N1)pdm09: 5 A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses have been antigenically characterised and 3 were similar to reference viruses representative of the A/Missouri/11/2025 (H1N1)pdm09-like Northern Hemisphere 2026/27 (H1N1)pdm09 vaccine strains. A(H3N2): 6 A(H3N2) viruses have been antigenically characterised and 6 were similar to reference viruses representative of the A/Darwin/1454/2025 (H3N2)-like and A/Darwin/1415/2025 (H3N2) like Northern Hemisphere 2026/27 (H3N2) vaccine strains. Influenza positive samples are screened for mutations in the virus neuraminidase ( NA ) and the cap-dependent endonuclease of the polymerase acidic protein (PA) genes known to confer neuraminidase inhibitor (oseltamivir and zanamivir) or baloxavir resistance, respectively. Results from this surveillance are given in table 4. There have been five detections with mutations related to reduced susceptibility/resistance to oseltamivir and/or reduced susceptibility to baloxavir. Data is presented on viral ARI incidents in different settings that are reported to UKHSA health protection teams ( HPTs ). Reporting practices are known to vary between seasons and between regions. Any interpretation of temporal and regional trends should consider the likelihood of differences in reporting of ARI incidents over time and between regions. There were 112 new ARI incidents reported in week 43 in England. These included: 101 incidents from care homes, of which 24 were due to SARS-CoV-2, 17 were due to influenza A, 4 were due to other pathogens, 3 were due to influenza (no type information available) and 3 were due to multiple pathogens. No pathogen was reported in 50 incidents 4 incidents from hospitals, of which 3 were due to influenza A and 1 was due to SARS-CoV-2 4 incidents from educational settings, of which 2 were due to influenza (no type information available) and 1 was due to other pathogens. No pathogen was reported in 1 incident 1 incident from prisons, of which 1 was due to SARS-CoV-2 2 incidents from other settings, of which 1 was due to SARS-CoV-2 and 1 was due to influenza (no type information available) Syndromic surveillance collects data from various healthcare sources where presentations are classified by patterns of symptoms compatible with specific infections. In some settings, the syndromic diagnosis can be supplemented by (rapid) testing. In this report, ED attendances are displayed. Further details and data from other syndromic surveillance systems can be found in the syndromic surveillance weekly summaries . During the week ending on 25 October 2026, ED attendances for acute respiratory infections increased and were similar to seasonally expected levels. ED attendances for COVID-19-like illness decreased. ED attendances for influenza-like illness increased and were above seasonally expected levels. ED attendance for acute bronchiolitis (a syndrome related to RSV infection) remained stable and below seasonally expected levels. Daily NHS 111 acute respiratory infection triaged calls remained stable. GP in-hours consultation rates for COVID-19 like consultations decreased, and other respiratory infection indicators remained stable. GP out-of-hours daily contacts for acute bronchitis/bronchiolitis increased but remained below seasonally expected levels overall. Note 6: 7-day moving average is adjusted for bank holidays. Grey columns show weekends and bank holidays. Note 7: the coloured line is the 7-day moving average by age group. Grey lines show the other age groups. The y-axis shows daily attendances. It is adjusted for bank holidays. Primary care surveillance is undertaken in collaboration with the Royal College of General Practitioners ( RCGP ) Research and Surveillance Centre ( RSC ), using a national sentinel surveillance system of around 2,000 GP practices covering over 20 million registered patients of all ages across England. More information on the methodology can be found in the data quality report . The weekly ILI consultation rate through the RCGP surveillance remained stable at 6.5 per 100,000 registered population in participating GP practices in week 43. This rate is in the baseline activity level (Figure 20). By age group, the highest rates were seen in those aged under 1 year (8.3 per 100,000), and those aged between 1 and 4 years (7.4 per 100,000). The lower respiratory tract infections ( LRTI ) consultation rate remained stable at 81.6 per 100,000 in week 43 compared with 81.9 per 100,000 in the previous week. news.content_original: This publication is licensed under the terms of the Open Government Licence v3.0 except where otherwise stated. To view this licence, visit nationalarchives.gov.uk/doc/open-government-licence/version/3 or write to the Information Policy Team, The National Archives, Kew, London TW9 4DU, or email: psi@nationalarchives.gov.uk . Where we have identified any third party copyright information you will need to obtain permission from the copyright holders concerned. This publication is available at https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/national-flu-and-covid-19-surveillance-reports-2026-to-2027-season/national-flu-and-covid-19-surveillance-report-29-october-2026-week-44 This report summarises the information from the surveillance systems which are used to monitor COVID-19 (caused by severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2)), influenza, respiratory syncytial virus ( RSV ) and diseases caused by other seasonal respiratory viruses in England. This report is based on data up to and including week 43 of 2026 (19 October and 25 October 2026). The main messages of this report are: Annual reports for the 2025 to 2026 season: Influenza in the UK, annual epidemiological report: winter 2025 to 2026 (published 28 May 2026) Epidemiology of COVID-19 in England (published 25 June 2026) Seasonal influenza vaccine uptake in all GP patients: annual report 2025 to 2026 (published 28 May 2026) Seasonal influenza vaccine uptake in school-aged children: annual report 2025 to 2026 (published 28 May 2026) Seasonal influenza vaccine uptake in frontline healthcare workers: annual report 2025 to 2026 (published 28 May 2026) Influenza activity was stable across most indicators and is circulating at low levels. Emergency department ( ED ) attendances for influenza-like-illness ( ILI ) increased and were above seasonally expected levels. The number of influenza-confirmed acute respiratory infection ( ARI ) incidents increased compared with the previous week. Weekly influenza vaccine uptake for the 2026 to 2027 season is reported for the fourth time this season. Data is for week 43 (up to 25 October 2026). Influenza vaccination data was unavailable or incomplete at the time of analysis in weeks 41 and 42, and led to several cohorts not being published in week 42. This has been corrected for this week’s report (week 43), and all cohorts are included. This will be corrected retrospectively in the report for week 42. There remains an issue that affects the attribution of vaccinations by provider setting. This is not expected to affect overall vaccination uptake estimates, which are considered to remain an accurate reflection of the influenza vaccination programme. Compared with the equivalent week last season (week 43 data, 2025 to 2026), vaccine uptake is lower among patients aged 65 years and over (53.6% vs 56.9%), patients aged 6 months to under 65 years in clinical risk groups (24.8% vs 26.2%), those aged 2 years (29.7% vs 30.8%), and those aged 3 years (29.5% vs 30.7%). Vaccine uptake is higher among pregnant women (29.1% vs 27.8%). COVID-19 activity decreased and is circulating at low levels. ED attendances for COVID-19-like illness decreased. The number of COVID-19 confirmed acute respiratory infections ( ARI ) incidents decreased compared with the previous week. By the end of week 43 2026, 42.5% of all people aged 75 years and over in England had been vaccinated with an autumn 2026 dose. Similarly, 18.2% of all people aged under 75 years with a weakened immune system in England had been vaccinated with an autumn 2026 dose since 1 October 2026. RSV activity increased and is circulating at baseline levels. ED attendances for acute bronchiolitis were stable and below seasonally expected levels. Note 1: these indicators use the moving epidemic method ( MEM ) and the mean standard deviation method ( MSD ) to define thresholds to determine their respective levels of activity. Further information on these methods can be found in Influenza surveillance in Europe: establishing epidemic thresholds by the Moving Epidemic Method and Setting thresholds to determine COVID-19 activity levels using the mean standard deviation ( MSD ) method, England, 2022 to 2024 . The MEM approach is well-established for some influenza surveillance indicators, however, for other indicators both the MEM and MSD are experimental and may be subject to future revision. Influenza laboratory surveillance and GP swabbing positivity have transitioned from using MEM to using MSD . These approaches will be considered alongside expert opinion and triangulation of other data sources. The Second Generation Surveillance System ( SGSS ) captures test result information for notifiable infectious diseases, including COVID-19 and influenza, from laboratories in England. The unified sample dataset ( USD ) stores all SARS-CoV-2 test results reported to SGSS , Respiratory DataMart and UKHSA laboratories, and is used to calculate the percentage of tests positive for SARS-CoV-2 among all SARS-CoV-2 tests conducted. As of 27 October 2026, there were a total of 1,847 COVID-19 cases identified in hospital settings in week 43, decreasing from 2,151 cases in the previous week. SARS-CoV-2 (COVID-19) PCR positivity in hospital settings decreased slightly in week 43, with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 8.3% up to Sunday 25 October 2026 compared with 8.8% for the same period on the previous Sunday. Positivity rates were highest among those aged 85 years and over with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 11.1% up to Sunday 25 October 2026. This has decreased compared to 13.0% in the same age group on the previous Sunday. Note 2: data from previous seasons is aligned by day. Note 3: testing policy and practice may change over time which can impact positivity rates, therefore comparisons over time should be interpreted with caution. Notable changes in testing policy occurred during 2022 to 2023, which are outlined in the data quality report . Note 4: the highlighted line corresponds to the age group in the subplot title, grey lines correspond to all other age groups. Influenza positivity remained stable in week 43, with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 6.6% up to Sunday 25 October 2026. This is compared with 6.4% on the previous Sunday. By type, influenza A positivity increased slightly in week 43, with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 5.8% up to Sunday 25 October 2026. Influenza B positivity increased in the same week, with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 0.3% up to Sunday 25 October 2026. Influenza A positivity rates were highest among those aged between 5 and 11 years, with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 16.6% up to Sunday 25 October 2026. This has increased from 11.3% in the same age group on the previous Sunday. Influenza B positivity rates for the same period were highest among those aged between 5 and 11 years, with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 1.8%. This has decreased from 2.3% in the same age group on the previous Sunday. RSV swab-positivity based PCR test results reported through SGSS have been included as a pilot indicator from week 49 2025 onwards. RSV positivity increased in week 43, with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 1.6% up to Sunday 25 October 2026, compared with 1.1% up to the previous Sunday. RSV positivity rates were highest in those aged between 0 and 4 years with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 10.1% up to Sunday 25 October 2026 in week 43. This has increased from 7.8% in the same age group on the previous Sunday. Respiratory DataMart is a sentinel laboratory-based surveillance system where participating laboratories report positive and negative test results for a number of respiratory viruses from samples primarily taken in hospital. A small proportion of primary care samples are also included in this reporting. In week 43, data is based on reporting from 9 out of the 14 sentinel laboratories. In week 43, 4,070 respiratory specimens reported through the Respiratory DataMart System were tested for influenza. There were 258 positive samples for influenza: 179 influenza A (not subtyped), 11 influenza A (H3N2), 51 influenza A (H1N1)pdm09, and 19 influenza B. Overall, influenza positivity increased slightly to 6.3% in week 43 compared with 5.9% in the previous week. In week 43, 4,952 respiratory specimens reported through the Respiratory DataMart System were tested for SARS-CoV-2. There were 376 positive samples for SARS-CoV-2. SARS-CoV-2 positivity remained stable at 7.6% compared with 7.3% in the previous week, with the highest positivity in those aged between 65 and 79 years at 10.0%. RSV positivity increased to 1.5%, with the highest positivity in those aged under 5 years at 8.3%. Adenovirus positivity increased to 1.5%, with the highest positivity in those aged under 5 years at 5.1%. Human metapneumovirus ( hMPV ) positivity decreased to 0.1%, with the highest positivity in those aged between 15 and 44 years at 0.4%. Parainfluenza positivity decreased slightly to 2.9%, with the highest positivity in those aged between 5 and 14 years at 11.3%. Rhinovirus positivity decreased slightly to 16.5%, with the highest positivity in those aged under 5 years at 29.1%. DataMart data is provisional and subject to retrospective updates. Note 5: shading represents 95% confidence intervals. This section is updated fortnightly. Data below was last updated in the week 43 report. UKHSA conducts genomic surveillance of SARS-CoV-2 lineages. This section provides an overview of circulating lineages in England, derived from data on sequenced PCR -positive SARS-CoV-2 samples in SGSS . The prevalence of UKHSA -designated lineages among sequenced cases is presented in Figure 13. To account for reporting delays, we report the proportion of lineages within COVID-19 cases that have had a sequenced positive sample between 14 September 2026 and 27 September 2026. Note that low sequencing numbers, especially within the latest reporting period, will impact the accuracy of the prevalence estimates. These most recent figures should therefore be interpreted with caution. Note that lineages will be grouped independently from their parent lineage once they reach sufficient prevalence, and may be re-grouped into their parent lineage if their prevalence subsequently falls. The data quality report contains more information on lineage groupings. Analysis of viruses from primary and secondary care shows that circulating A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses show low genetic diversity and all belong to clade D.3.1.1. Observations published from the WHO influenza vaccine composition meeting (VCM) in September 2026 suggest low reactivity of some viruses within the D.3.1.1 subclade with post-infection ferret antisera raised against A/Missouri/11/2025 (H1N1)pdm09-like virus – the A(H1N1)pdm09 component in 2026 Southern and 2026/2027 Northern Hemisphere cell- and egg-based influenza vaccines - and human sera post-vaccination with the Southern Hemisphere vaccine 2026. It is not yet clear how vaccine effectiveness against clinical disease may be affected by these observations. Vaccines typically still provide protection against severe clinical disease when drifted strains are seen with only a modest reduction in effectiveness. The characterisation of circulating A(H3N2) viruses shows that A(H3N2) viruses are currently showing low genetic diversity. All sequenced viruses to date belong to genetic subclade K. To date, only a small number of influenza B viruses have been detected, which show some genetic diversity. Between week 35 2026 (week ending 30 August 2026) and week 43 2026 (week ending 25 October 2026), the UKHSA respiratory virus unit ( RVU ) has genetically characterised 297 seasonal influenza viruses, and identified 184 influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses, 86 influenza A(H3N2) viruses, and 27 influenza B viruses. Details of the characterised viruses by subtype are shown in Tables 1, 2 and 3. The RVU has confirmed by genome sequencing the detection of live attenuated influenza vaccine ( LAIV ) viruses in 11 influenza A/B positive samples, collected from children aged between 2 and 16 years. UKHSA RVU performs antigenic characterisation of influenza A(H1N1)pdm09, influenza A(H3N2) and influenza B viruses using haemagglutination inhibition ( HI ) assays. Data from these assays are used to compare how similar the currently circulating influenza viruses are to the strains included in seasonal influenza vaccines, and to monitor for changes in circulating influenza viruses. Similarity of currently circulating influenza strains to vaccine strains is defined as having an antibody titre within 4-fold when compared with reference viruses representative of the vaccine strain. Antigenic characterisation of viruses in the current reporting period is underway. A(H1N1)pdm09: 5 A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses have been antigenically characterised and 3 were similar to reference viruses representative of the A/Missouri/11/2025 (H1N1)pdm09-like Northern Hemisphere 2026/27 (H1N1)pdm09 vaccine strains. A(H3N2): 6 A(H3N2) viruses have been antigenically characterised and 6 were similar to reference viruses representative of the A/Darwin/1454/2025 (H3N2)-like and A/Darwin/1415/2025 (H3N2) like Northern Hemisphere 2026/27 (H3N2) vaccine strains. Influenza positive samples are screened for mutations in the virus neuraminidase ( NA ) and the cap-dependent endonuclease of the polymerase acidic protein (PA) genes known to confer neuraminidase inhibitor (oseltamivir and zanamivir) or baloxavir resistance, respectively. Results from this surveillance are given in table 4. There have been five detections with mutations related to reduced susceptibility/resistance to oseltamivir and/or reduced susceptibility to baloxavir. Data is presented on viral ARI incidents in different settings that are reported to UKHSA health protection teams ( HPTs ). Reporting practices are known to vary between seasons and between regions. Any interpretation of temporal and regional trends should consider the likelihood of differences in reporting of ARI incidents over time and between regions. There were 112 new ARI incidents reported in week 43 in England. These included: 101 incidents from care homes, of which 24 were due to SARS-CoV-2, 17 were due to influenza A, 4 were due to other pathogens, 3 were due to influenza (no type information available) and 3 were due to multiple pathogens. No pathogen was reported in 50 incidents 4 incidents from hospitals, of which 3 were due to influenza A and 1 was due to SARS-CoV-2 4 incidents from educational settings, of which 2 were due to influenza (no type information available) and 1 was due to other pathogens. No pathogen was reported in 1 incident 1 incident from prisons, of which 1 was due to SARS-CoV-2 2 incidents from other settings, of which 1 was due to SARS-CoV-2 and 1 was due to influenza (no type information available) Syndromic surveillance collects data from various healthcare sources where presentations are classified by patterns of symptoms compatible with specific infections. In some settings, the syndromic diagnosis can be supplemented by (rapid) testing. In this report, ED attendances are displayed. Further details and data from other syndromic surveillance systems can be found in the syndromic surveillance weekly summaries . During the week ending on 25 October 2026, ED attendances for acute respiratory infections increased and were similar to seasonally expected levels. ED attendances for COVID-19-like illness decreased. ED attendances for influenza-like illness increased and were above seasonally expected levels. ED attendance for acute bronchiolitis (a syndrome related to RSV infection) remained stable and below seasonally expected levels. Daily NHS 111 acute respiratory infection triaged calls remained stable. GP in-hours consultation rates for COVID-19 like consultations decreased, and other respiratory infection indicators remained stable. GP out-of-hours daily contacts for acute bronchitis/bronchiolitis increased but remained below seasonally expected levels overall. Note 6: 7-day moving average is adjusted for bank holidays. Grey columns show weekends and bank holidays. Note 7: the coloured line is the 7-day moving average by age group. Grey lines show the other age groups. The y-axis shows daily attendances. It is adjusted for bank holidays. Primary care surveillance is undertaken in collaboration with the Royal College of General Practitioners ( RCGP ) Research and Surveillance Centre ( RSC ), using a national sentinel surveillance system of around 2,000 GP practices covering over 20 million registered patients of all ages across England. More information on the methodology can be found in the data quality report . The weekly ILI consultation rate through the RCGP surveillance remained stable at 6.5 per 100,000 registered population in participating GP practices in week 43. This rate is in the baseline activity level (Figure 20). By age group, the highest rates were seen in those aged under 1 year (8.3 per 100,000), and those aged between 1 and 4 years (7.4 per 100,000). analysis.time: The report covers data up to and including week 43 of 2026 (19 October and 25 October 2026).
analysis.location_and_population: England, with data on influenza, RSV, and COVID-19 activity across different age groups and populations.
analysis.event: The report details the surveillance findings for influenza, RSV, and COVID-19 in England during week 43 of 2026, including ED attendances, confirmed ARI cases, and vaccine uptake data.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Influenza activity was stable and circulating at low levels, with increased ED attendances for ILI above seasonally expected levels. RSV activity increased and was at baseline levels. COVID-19 activity decreased, with lower ED attendances for COVID-19-like illness and fewer confirmed ARI cases compared to the previous week. Vaccine uptake data showed some variations among age groups and risk categories.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The report is based on data up to week 43, with some vaccination data missing in weeks 41 and 42. The methods used for defining activity levels (MEM and MSD) are noted as experimental and may be subject to revision. The data is considered accurate for overall vaccination uptake estimates.

analysis.brief_en: The National Flu and COVID-19 Surveillance Report for 29 October 2026 (week 44) provides an overview of influenza, RSV, and COVID-19 activity in England up to week 43. Influenza activity remained stable, with increased emergency department (ED) attendances for influenza-like illness (ILI) above seasonally expected levels. RSV activity increased, while COVID-19 activity decreased, with fewer confirmed acute respiratory infection (ARI) cases compared to the previous week. Vaccine uptake data for the 2026-2027 season showed lower rates among older adults and those in clinical risk groups, but higher uptake among pregnant women. Some data was missing in earlier weeks due to incomplete vaccination records, but this was corrected in week 43. The report notes that the methods used to define activity levels are experimental and may be revised. Overall, the influenza vaccination programme is considered to reflect accurate uptake estimates despite some limitations in data collection.

news.content: English Login Homepage Topic News Political System Destination Event Travel Happy Vietnam Enterprise Product Heritage Museum Figure Multimedia Data Home Culture – Society Y tế Seasonal influenza increases the risk of heart attack and stroke. Seasonal influenza can cause serious complications beyond the respiratory tract, including myocardial infarction, stroke, and heart failure. The risk is particularly noteworthy in the elderly, those with cardiovascular disease, or those with chronic illnesses. Báo Đầu tư•29/10/2026 Follow Vietnam.vn on Google Add Vietnam.vn on Google 0 Cardiologists warn that influenza infection can be a contributing factor to heart attacks and strokes, especially in individuals with pre-existing vascular damage or poorly controlled underlying conditions. Worryingly, the risk of complications can increase even in the early days of illness, requiring close monitoring of the patient's health. Seasonal influenza can cause serious complications beyond the respiratory tract, including myocardial infarction, stroke, and heart failure. The risk is particularly noteworthy in the elderly, those with cardiovascular disease, or those with chronic illnesses. Associate Professor Tran Song Giang, Deputy Director of the Cardiovascular Institute at Bach Mai Hospital, said that influenza virus infection can trigger a systemic inflammatory response, causing changes in blood clotting, vascular function, and the ability to supply oxygen to organs. In individuals with pre-existing atherosclerosis, the inflammatory response can make atherosclerotic plaques less stable, increasing the risk of rupture of the outer layer. This process can trigger the formation of blood clots, causing blockages in the flow of blood within the artery. If a blood clot blocks a coronary artery, the patient is at risk of a heart attack. If the blockage occurs in a blood vessel supplying the brain, the consequence can be an ischemic stroke. This mechanism explains why a respiratory infection can become a trigger for dangerous circulatory events, especially in the elderly or patients with pre-existing vascular damage. Khám phá thêm Tìm hiểu lịch sử Đọc Mẹo Du Lịch Khám phá ĐNA Beyond just causing inflammation, influenza also increases the workload on the heart. During infection, body temperature rises, and the heart rate often increases, leading to increased oxygen consumption by the heart muscle. Associate Professor Tran Song Giang also noted that in some cases, the influenza virus can be associated with myocardial damage, causing myocarditis and affecting the heart's ability to contract. Of particular concern is that cardiovascular events don't only occur in people already diagnosed with heart disease. Individuals with no prior history of cardiovascular disease can still experience complications during influenza infection, although the risk is influenced by age, health status, and pre-existing risk factors. Studies presented by Associate Professor Dr. Tran Song Giang show a notable correlation between influenza infection and acute cardiovascular events. Several studies have noted that the risk of myocardial infarction may increase by approximately 6-10 times, while the risk of stroke increases by approximately 3-10 times during certain periods following influenza infection. These figures reflect the relative risk increase observed in specific studies and do not mean that all patients with influenza are at a higher risk of heart attack or stroke. You may also like Nevertheless, research shows that influenza should not be taken lightly, especially for those with pre-existing cardiovascular risk factors. Proactive prevention and early detection of abnormal symptoms are crucial in limiting complications. The elderly are a group that requires special attention due to their weakened immune response, while the incidence of chronic diseases is often higher than in younger people. Given the risks associated with influenza infection, experts emphasize the importance of prevention, especially for the elderly and those with underlying health conditions. Annual flu vaccination is one of the important measures to reduce the risk of contracting the flu and the serious complications it causes. Vaccination should be administered according to age, health status, and professional guidance. However, vaccination does not completely eliminate the possibility of contracting the flu or experiencing complications. People still need to maintain health protection measures, especially during periods when the flu virus is circulating widely. Along with vaccination, personal hygiene measures such as frequent handwashing, covering your mouth when coughing or sneezing, wearing a mask when experiencing respiratory symptoms, keeping living spaces well-ventilated, and limiting close contact with sick people remain important in reducing the risk of infection. Experts note that cardiovascular complications related to influenza can appear even during the acute phase of the illness, so monitoring should not focus solely on fever, cough, or sore throat. According to Dr. Nguyen Van My of the Long Chau Vaccination System, the protective efficacy of the flu vaccine under suitable conditions can reach approximately 90%, but the actual level of protection varies depending on the circulating virus strain, age, and health status of the vaccinated individual. The protective ability can also decrease over time, while the flu virus is constantly mutating and new circulating strains are emerging. Therefore, annual flu vaccination is crucial in maintaining protection, especially for young children, the elderly, pregnant women, people with chronic diseases, and those with weakened immune systems. According to Doctor Nguyen Van My, the body usually needs about two weeks after vaccination to develop a protective immune response. Therefore, people should proactively get vaccinated before the flu season or as soon as conditions permit, instead of waiting until the number of cases increases before getting vaccinated. You may also like According to experts, vaccines do not guarantee absolute prevention of all cases of influenza, but they play an important role in reducing the risk of illness and limiting serious consequences. Complete and timely vaccination, including annual booster shots, can contribute to reducing the risk of pneumonia, respiratory failure, hospitalization, and death from influenza. Besides vaccination, the Ministry of Health recommends that people wear masks correctly in healthcare facilities, on public transport, in crowded places, or in enclosed spaces with poor ventilation. People with respiratory symptoms should limit close contact with others and proactively take time off from school or work to avoid infection. Washing hands frequently with soap, covering your mouth and nose when coughing or sneezing, regularly cleaning frequently touched surfaces, and keeping your living space well-ventilated also help reduce the risk of virus transmission. For children with the flu, parents should pay attention to symptoms such as difficulty breathing, rapid breathing, cyanosis, lethargy, seizures, signs of dehydration, or a worsening of the condition after a period of apparent improvement. These are signs that require prompt medical attention and treatment; self-treatment at home should not be prolonged. The Department of Disease Prevention also advises people not to self-medicate with antiviral or antibiotic drugs without a prescription from a healthcare professional. Individuals in high-risk groups should contact a healthcare facility early if they experience suspicious symptoms to receive appropriate advice, assessment, and treatment. news.content: English Login Homepage Topic News Political System Destination Event Travel Happy Vietnam Enterprise Product Heritage Museum Figure Multimedia Data Home Culture – Society Y tế Seasonal influenza can cause serious complications in children; parents should proactively take preventive measures. Seasonal influenza can cause serious complications, even death, in otherwise healthy children. Doctors advise parents to recognize early signs of worsening symptoms and proactively take annual flu precautions for their children. Báo Tin Tức•28/10/2026 Follow Vietnam.vn on Google Add Vietnam.vn on Google 0 From fever and cough to cardiogenic shock and severe respiratory failure. Seasonal influenza is easily spread in schools, daycare centers, and other communal living environments. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), the world records an estimated one billion cases of seasonal influenza each year, including 3-5 million severe cases. A 7-year-old child in critical condition due to influenza A causing acute pulmonary edema, fulminant myocarditis, and cardiogenic shock is being treated at Children's Hospital 1. Photo: Provided by the hospital. In early October, Children's Hospital 2 ( Ho Chi Minh City) recorded an average of over 2,300 respiratory examinations per day. At Children's Hospital 1, respiratory illnesses accounted for approximately 70% of total examinations, with the main causative agents including seasonal influenza, adenovirus, and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). Khám phá thêm Tìm hiểu lịch sử Đọc Mẹo Du Lịch Khám phá ĐNA Associate Professor Dr. Pham Van Quang, Head of the Intensive Care and Toxicology Department at Children's Hospital 1, said that seasonal influenza is usually caused by influenza A and B viruses. The disease starts suddenly with fever, chills, headache, muscle aches, fatigue, dry cough, sore throat, nasal congestion or runny nose. Children may also experience nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. Most patients experience fever for 3-5 days and then recover, while the cough may last longer. However, some cases can progress severely, causing pneumonia, myocarditis, cardiovascular collapse, liver and kidney damage, and be life-threatening. The hospital once admitted a 7-year-old child in critical condition due to influenza A causing acute pulmonary edema, fulminant myocarditis, and cardiogenic shock. The day before admission, the child had a dry cough, runny nose, and persistent high fever that responded poorly to antipyretics. The following morning, the child continued to have a fever, felt weak, and had difficulty breathing. The family took the child to Vung Tau General Hospital and then transferred him to Children's Hospital 1. Upon admission, the child was cyanotic, in cardiovascular collapse, and suffering from severe respiratory failure. Doctors had to use ECMO, an extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) system, combined with continuous hemodialysis, hypothermia to protect the brain, and treatment for excessive inflammation. After nearly 12 days, the child was weaned off ECMO and mechanical ventilation; respiratory, cardiovascular, and other organ functions gradually recovered. According to Dr. Truong Huu Khanh, Vice President of the Ho Chi Minh City Infectious Diseases Association, seasonal influenza can cause serious complications even in healthy children. Besides pneumonia and respiratory failure, children may develop encephalitis, altered consciousness, coma, myocarditis, or bacterial superinfection leading to sepsis, shock, and multiple organ failure. You may also like Some children who survive severe complications may suffer from lasting effects on motor skills, memory, and cognition. Meanwhile, initial symptoms such as fever, cough, runny nose, and fatigue are easily mistaken for a common cold, causing parents to be slow to recognize when the illness has progressed to a serious stage. Dr. Quang noted that children should be taken to the hospital immediately if they experience difficulty breathing, rapid breathing, labored breathing, chest pain, cyanosis, altered consciousness, or if they have cold hands and feet, mottled skin, a rapid and weak pulse. Parents should not self-medicate their children with antiviral or antibiotic drugs due to the risk of side effects and drug resistance. More flu prevention options for children According to Dr. Truong Huu Khanh, many countries have included annual flu vaccination in their public health protection strategies. Children with the flu can transmit the virus within families and schools, increasing the risk of infection for the elderly and those with underlying health conditions. Therefore, flu prevention for children also helps reduce the risk of infection for family members. On October 28th, VNVC Vaccination System launched the AstraZeneca (UK) nasal spray flu vaccine, becoming the first vaccination center in Vietnam to offer this vaccine. Photo: VNVC Dr. Bach Thi Chinh, Medical Director of the VNVC Vaccination System, said that children often have close contact with friends at school and daycare, making them susceptible to illness and bringing viruses home. Preventive measures need to be maintained annually. In addition to injectable vaccines, on October 28th, VNVC launched the AstraZeneca (UK) nasal spray flu vaccine for children aged 2 to under 18 years old. The vaccine is delivered directly into the nasal mucosa, providing an alternative option for children who are afraid of needles. According to Dr. Chinh, this is a live attenuated vaccine that protects against three strains of the virus: A/H1N1, A/H3N2, and B/Victoria. The vaccine has undergone more than 20 years of safety monitoring and has been deployed in 34 countries and territories, with over 200 million doses distributed. The vaccine stimulates an immune response in the nasal and throat mucosa, where influenza viruses typically enter; it generates antibodies through systemic immunity and stimulates cellular immunity, helping to identify and eliminate virus-infected cells. According to research data presented by the organization, the vaccine's effectiveness in preventing influenza reaches 88% against virus strains similar to those in the vaccine. AstraZeneca experts note that, although needle-free, spray vaccines must still be administered by healthcare professionals or under professional supervision. Children need to be screened, appropriately prescribed, and vaccination safety procedures must be followed. You may also like Spray vaccines need to be stored at very low temperatures, between -20 and -30 degrees Celsius. Photo: VVNC According to information from VNVC, this vaccine is stored at a temperature of -20 to -30 degrees Celsius. Before use, the product is thawed according to the procedure, then stored at 2-8 degrees Celsius for a maximum of 15 weeks as instructed by the manufacturer. Proper storage requires specialized cold storage, continuous temperature monitoring systems, and shelf life control. These requirements must be maintained throughout transportation, distribution, and use to ensure vaccine quality. Dr. Khanh noted that the nasal spray vaccine is an additional preventative option, making it easier for parents to protect their children from the flu. "Regardless of the method used, proactively preventing the flu annually remains essential to reduce the risk of illness and related complications," the doctor emphasized. news.title_zh: 季节性流感可导致儿童严重并发症;家长应积极采取预防措施。- 越南.vn
news.source_body_en: The article from Vietnam.vn, published on 2026-10-28, highlights the risks of seasonal influenza in children, emphasizing that it can lead to severe complications such as acute pulmonary edema, fulminant myocarditis, and cardiogenic shock. A 7-year-old child was admitted to Children's Hospital 1 in critical condition, with symptoms including high fever, difficulty breathing, and cyanosis. The hospital reported an average of over 2,300 respiratory examinations per day in early October, with seasonal influenza being a primary cause. Doctors at Children's Hospital 1 noted that the disease can progress rapidly, even in healthy children, and advised parents to seek immediate medical attention if symptoms worsen. The article also discusses the importance of annual flu prevention, including the recent launch of the AstraZeneca nasal spray vaccine for children aged 2 to under 18. This vaccine, which targets A/H1N1, A/H3N2, and B/Victoria strains, has been used in 34 countries and has undergone over 20 years of safety monitoring. The article underscores the need for parents to recognize early signs of severe illness and avoid self-medicating children with antiviral or antibiotic drugs.

news.content_title: Vaccination campaign against seasonal influenza starts on Monday
news.content: EN MT News Current Affairs Foreign Affairs European Union Sport TVMi LIVE TVM TVM+ TVMSport+ Magic Radju Malta Radju Malta 2 JOBS Current Affairs Vaccination campaign against seasonal influenza starts on Monday by TVM Newsroom October 30, 2026 October 30, 2026 Aqra bil- Malti The campaign will offer free vaccinations against seasonal influenza, COVID-19, and pneumococcal disease to eligible persons. Vaccination remains one of the most effective ways to reduce the risk of serious illness and complications from respiratory infections, particularly during the winter months. The Deputy Prime Minister, who was one of the first to be vaccinated, urged the Maltese and Gozitans to follow suit. Dr Borg thanked all staff at the Ministry and health professionals, who worked for the vaccines to be available on time despite international challenges, and for the vaccination service to be provided in the best possible way. “The Health Ministry will start the seasonal vaccination on Monday.I urge all those who normally get vaccinated to do so again, as this is important for them and for those around them. I also urge those considering getting vaccinated for the first time to get informed, make the decision and come forward to be vaccinated,” Sr Borg said. This year, the service will be available at Health Centres in Malta and Gozo, National Immunisation clinics for children, adolescents and pregnant women, and participating Local Councils, as well as doctors in the private sector who obtain vaccines purchased by the Government. The public is urged to make use of the service most convenient or them. The Government is offering these vaccines at no charge as follows: Vaccine against seasonal influenza, available to persons over the age of six months; Vaccine against COVID-19, available to persons over the age of six months; PCV20 against pneumococcus, for 60+ adults as well as adults under the age of 60 suffering from medical conditions that make them eligible. The PCV20 vaccine is only administered once, meaning that those who have already taken it need not take it again. The three vaccines can be taken on the same day, according to the clinical availability of the person and the evaluation of the administering health professional. From 2 November, adults and adolescents from age 13+ can attend at Health Centre treatment rooms and no appointment is needed for the times and places indicated below. Between Sunday and Friday, including public holidays but excluding Saturdays, vaccinations will be administered between 1.00 p.m. and 7.00 p.m. at these centres: Cospicua Health Centre; Birkirkara Health Centre; Ħal Qormi Health Centre; Rabat, Malta Heakth Centre.. From Monday to Sunday, including Saturdays, Sundays and public holidays, vaccinations will be adminiwtered between 1.00 p.m. and 7.00 p.m. at these centres: Mosta Health Centre; Paola Health Centre; Floriana Health Centre; Gżira Health Centre; ; Ħal Kirkop Health Centre; Rabat, Gozo Health Centre. All those attending should present a valid Identity Card. Vaccination against pneumococcus is available regularly for 60+ adults. Vulnerable adults under the age of 60 need a medical certificate confirming their eligibility for this vaccination. There will be special sessions for vaccination of babies, children and adolescents, aged between six months and 12 years, as well as for pregnant women, at these clinics: For Malta: National Immunisation Service Clinic at Floriana; For Gozo: National Immunisation Clinic at Rabat, Gozo No appointments are needed for these clinics. The service will be available between 7.30 a.m. and 2.00 p.m. on the ollowing dates: Saturday, 7 and Sunday 8 November; Saturday, 14 and Sunday 15 November; Saturday, 21 and Sunday 22 November; Saturday, 28 and Sunday 29 November; Saturday, 5 and Sunday 6 December; Saturday, 12 and Sunday, 13 December; Sunday, 27, Monday, 28, Tuesday, 29 and Wednesday, 30 December. Parents or legal guardians accompanying the children are expected to carry with them: The ID Card for the parent or legal guardian; The booklet for the child is known as the Baby Booklet. Sessions for seasonal vaccination are also being organised this year through participating local councils, thus making the vaccination service more accessible in communities. As arrangements and dates may vary from one locality to another, the public is urged to contact their Local Council to confirm participation and get details about the date, time and location of the session. Doctors working in private practice may obtain supplies of vaccines against influenza, COVID-19 and pneumococcus purchased by the Government to administer to eligible patients in their private practice. Patients wishing to get the vaccine through their family doctor or another doctor in private practice can contact their doctor directly to verify whether this service is being offered. Influenza, COVID-19 and infections from pneumococcus can lead to serious complications, particularly among the elderly, children in the six-month to five-year group, those with chronic medical conditions, pregnant women, health service workers and other vulnerable people. The current monitoring in Malta indicates an increase in illnesses with symptoms similar to influenza as soon as the respiratory infection season starts, although levels generally remain similar to those registered in the same period in previous seasons. No increase related to hospital admissions has been registered so far. The epidemiologic situation will continue to be monitored during autumn and winter. The health authorities say the public should not put off getting vaccinated until respiratory infections spread. Vaccination before the increase in circulation of these infections in winter allows the body to develop protection and helps to reduce the risk of serious illness. Protect yourself and those around you – get vaccinated this winter. Less influenza, more time for yourself! Visit the influenza.gov.mt website for more information. From Monday to Sunday, including Saturdays, Sundays and public holidays, vaccinations will be adminiwtered between 1.00 p.m. and 7.00 p.m. at these centres: Mosta Health Centre; Paola Health Centre; Floriana Health Centre; Gżira Health Centre; ; Ħal Kirkop Health Centre; Rabat, Gozo Health Centre. All those attending should present a valid Identity Card. Vaccination against pneumococcus is available regularly for 60+ adults. Vulnerable adults under the age of 60 need a medical certificate confirming their eligibility for this vaccination. There will be special sessions for vaccination of babies, children and adolescents, aged between six months and 12 years, as well as for pregnant women, at these clinics: For Malta: National Immunisation Service Clinic at Floriana; For Gozo: National Immunisation Clinic at Rabat, Gozo No appointments are needed for these clinics. The service will be available between 7.30 a.m. and 2.00 p.m. on the ollowing dates: Saturday, 7 and Sunday 8 November; Saturday, 14 and Sunday 15 November; Saturday, 21 and Sunday 22 November; Saturday, 28 and Sunday 29 November; Saturday, 5 and Sunday 6 December; Saturday, 12 and Sunday, 13 December; Sunday, 27, Monday, 28, Tuesday, 29 and Wednesday, 30 December. Parents or legal guardians accompanying the children are expected to carry with them: The ID Card for the parent or legal guardian; The booklet for the child is known as the Baby Booklet. Sessions for seasonal vaccination are also being organised this year through participating local councils, thus making the vaccination service more accessible in communities. As arrangements and dates may vary from one locality to another, the public is urged to contact their Local Council to confirm participation and get details about the date, time and location of the session. Doctors working in private practice may obtain supplies of vaccines against influenza, COVID-19 and pneumococcus purchased by the Government to administer to eligible patients in their private practice. Patients wishing to get the vaccine through their family doctor or another doctor in private practice can contact their doctor directly to verify whether this service is being offered. Influenza, COVID-19 and infections from pneumococcus can lead to serious complications, particularly among the elderly, children in the six-month to five-year group, those with chronic medical conditions, pregnant women, health service workers and other vulnerable people. The current monitoring in Malta indicates an increase in illnesses with symptoms similar to influenza as soon as the respiratory infection season starts, although levels generally remain similar to those registered in the same period in previous seasons. No increase related to hospital admissions has been registered so far. The epidemiologic situation will continue to be monitored during autumn and winter. The health authorities say the public should not put off getting vaccinated until respiratory infections spread. Vaccination before the increase in circulation of these infections in winter allows the body to develop protection and helps to reduce the risk of serious illness. Protect yourself and those around you – get vaccinated this winter. Less influenza, more time for yourself! Visit the influenza.gov.mt website for more information. news.content_title: Early Flu Season Is Here! Hospitalizations Hit a 16-Year High
news.content: Go Ad-Free Cart0Login The People's Perspective on Medicine Drug Information Home Remedies Health Concerns Libraries Podcasts Health eGuides Store Early Flu Season Is Here! Hospitalizations Hit a 16-Year High Hospitalizations are rising in this early flu season as H1N1 dominates. What can Australia and South Korea teach us? What can you do? 4.4 - 16 ratings Influenza (flu) Joe Graedon October 29, 2026 1 Comment Joe Graedon - October 29, 2026 - 1 Comment Influenza does not usually command much attention before Halloween. Many people don’t contemplate a flu shot until a week or two before Thanksgiving. Then they get worried about traveling to family get-togethers. This year is different, though. An early flu season is already showing up in laboratory tests, emergency rooms and hospital admissions. Although influenza activity remains relatively low nationwide, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention is reporting that flu activity has been climbing since late August or early September. The strain hitting early and hard is A(H1N1), which is quite different from the influenza A(H3N2/subclade-K) that affected Australia and New Zealand during the 2026 winter in the Southern Hemisphere. Those countries experienced a relatively subdued flu season. Influenza got off to a slow start down under, and overall activity remained substantially lower than in 2025.. Our Early Warning System Failed Us We frequently look to Australia and New Zealand for an early warning about what we should expect six months later in the Northern Hemisphere. It turns out that we should have been studying South Korea instead. It was the canary in the coal mine. Scientists there were reporting H1N1pdm09 by August and early September. Hospitalizations climbed rapidly. Guess what is hitting the United States. You got it: H1N1pdm09. And just as in South Korea, hospitalizations are climbing. During the week ending October 17, the CDC’s influenza hospitalization surveillance system recorded an unusually high hospitalization rate for this early in the season, somewhat reminiscent of what was observed in South Korea. No one is panicking, but it is the highest hospitalization rate for this point in the flu season since 2010-2011. An Early Flu Season Is Showing Up in Several Ways The hospitalization numbers are not the only warning sign. The percentage of specimens testing positive for influenza has been increasing. So have emergency department visits involving flu and laboratory-confirmed influenza hospitalizations. During the week ending October 17, hospitals participating in the CDC’s National Healthcare Safety Network reported 4,811 laboratory-confirmed influenza admissions. The hospitalization rate was highest among people 65 and older. There is also evidence that influenza is getting an unusually early start in certain parts of the country. Louisiana and Hawaii had reached “moderate” levels of influenza-like illness activity while most states were still categorized as low or minimal. Walgreens has reported another intriguing signal. Based on testing, antiviral prescriptions and sales of cold and flu products, the pharmacy chain estimated that flu activity was running roughly four weeks ahead of recent flu seasons. That doesn’t mean we are headed for a disastrous winter. It does mean that influenza may not be waiting until December or January to make its presence felt. New York Flu Cases Jump Sharply New York provides a dramatic example. More than 3,500 laboratory-confirmed flu cases were reported during the week ending October 17. That was roughly a 400 percent increase compared with the corresponding week last year, according to state health data. A percentage increase like that can sound scarier than it really is when starting numbers are small. Nevertheless, combined with the national hospitalization data, it reinforces the message that influenza is appearing earlier than usual this fall. H1N1 Dominates This Early Flu Season So far, this is overwhelmingly an influenza A season. Of 323 influenza viruses reported by public health laboratories during the week ending October 17, 318 were influenza A and only five were influenza B. Even more striking, among the influenza A viruses that were subtyped, 239 of 241, or 99.2 percent, were influenza A(H1N1)pdm09. None were ordinary seasonal H3N2. The H1N1 viruses circulating now are descendants of the virus that emerged during the 2009 pandemic. They have been circulating as seasonal influenza viruses ever since. There is a wrinkle. The CDC reports that recently circulating H1N1 viruses belong predominantly to a group called D.3.1.1 and are continuing to undergo genetic changes. Does that mean this year’s flu vaccine will be a poor match? At this point, nobody knows. The CDC states: “It is too early to know what viruses may predominate or to say whether there might be implications on flu vaccine effectiveness this season.” That uncertainty is worth keeping in mind. Influenza viruses are moving targets, and vaccine effectiveness varies from year to year. This year’s shots may be good...but they are never perfect. We have been tracking effectiveness since 2004. Here is a link to our analysis. Over that time period, the influenza vaccine effectiveness has averaged 40%. Some may think that’s pretty good. I would have hoped for something a lot better. Is Now the Time to Get a Flu Shot? For people who plan to get vaccinated against influenza this year, the clock is ticking. The CDC recommends annual influenza vaccination for nearly everyone six months of age and older. For most people, September or October is considered an ideal time. There is also a practical reason not to wait much longer. It generally takes about two weeks after vaccination for the immune response to develop. A vaccination around Halloween should therefore provide time for an immune response before Thanksgiving travel and family gatherings. People 65 and older deserve particular attention. They currently have the highest influenza hospitalization rate, and the CDC preferentially recommends one of three vaccines for this age group: a high-dose vaccine, an adjuvanted vaccine or a recombinant vaccine. Vaccination cannot guarantee that someone won’t catch influenza. The CDC itself acknowledges that vaccinated people can still become infected and transmit flu. A much bigger question involves whether a flu shot reduces the severity of an infection if someone catches influenza. Some observational studies have found lower rates of intensive-care admission, organ failure or death among vaccinated people who nevertheless develop laboratory-confirmed influenza. Other studies, however, have found little or no reduction in severity. Because these comparisons are observational rather than randomized, they cannot completely rule out differences between vaccinated and unvaccinated patients that might influence the outcome. Bottom line: Flu shots moderately reduce the likelihood of catching the flu and might reduce the intensity of the infection. What can you do? 4.4 - 16 ratings Influenza (flu) Joe Graedon October 29, 2026 1 Comment Joe Graedon - October 29, 2026 - 1 Comment Influenza does not usually command much attention before Halloween. Many people don’t contemplate a flu shot until a week or two before Thanksgiving. Then they get worried about traveling to family get-togethers. This year is different, though. An early flu season is already showing up in laboratory tests, emergency rooms and hospital admissions. Although influenza activity remains relatively low nationwide, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention is reporting that flu activity has been climbing since late August or early September. The strain hitting early and hard is A(H1N1), which is quite different from the influenza A(H3N2/subclade-K) that affected Australia and New Zealand during the 2026 winter in the Southern Hemisphere. Those countries experienced a relatively subdued flu season. Influenza got off to a slow start down under, and overall activity remained substantially lower than in 2025.. Our Early Warning System Failed Us We frequently look to Australia and New Zealand for an early warning about what we should expect six months later in the Northern Hemisphere. It turns out that we should have been studying South Korea instead. It was the canary in the coal mine. Scientists there were reporting H1N1pdm09 by August and early September. Hospitalizations climbed rapidly. Guess what is hitting the United States. You got it: H1N1pdm09. And just as in South Korea, hospitalizations are climbing. During the week ending October 17, the CDC’s influenza hospitalization surveillance system recorded an unusually high hospitalization rate for this early in the season, somewhat reminiscent of what was observed in South Korea. No one is panicking, but it is the highest hospitalization rate for this point in the flu season since 2010-2011. So have emergency department visits involving flu and laboratory-confirmed influenza hospitalizations. During the week ending October 17, hospitals participating in the CDC’s National Healthcare Safety Network reported 4,811 laboratory-confirmed influenza admissions. Louisiana and Hawaii had reached “moderate” levels of influenza-like illness activity while most states were still categorized as low or minimal. Walgreens has reported another intriguing signal. Based on testing, antiviral prescriptions and sales of cold and flu products, the pharmacy chain estimated that flu activity was running roughly four weeks ahead of recent flu seasons. A percentage increase like that can sound scarier than it really is when starting numbers are small. Does that mean this year’s flu vaccine will be a poor match? At this point, nobody knows. The CDC states: “It is too early to know what viruses may predominate or to say whether there might be implications on flu vaccine effectiveness this season.” That uncertainty is worth keeping in mind. Influenza viruses are moving targets, and vaccine effectiveness varies from year to year. This year’s shots may be good...but they are never perfect. We have been tracking effectiveness since 2004. Here is a link to our analysis. Over that time period, the influenza vaccine effectiveness has averaged 40%. Some may think that’s pretty good. I would have hoped for something a lot better. The CDC recommends annual influenza vaccination for nearly everyone six months of age and older. For most people, September or October is considered an ideal time. A vaccination around Halloween should therefore provide time for an immune response before Thanksgiving travel and family gatherings. People 65 and older deserve particular attention. They currently have the highest influenza hospitalization rate, and the CDC preferentially recommends one of three vaccines for this age group: a high-dose vaccine, an adjuvanted vaccine or a recombinant vaccine. Vaccination cannot guarantee that someone won’t catch influenza. The CDC itself acknowledges that vaccinated people can still become infected and transmit flu. A much bigger question involves whether a flu shot reduces the severity of an infection if someone catches influenza.
